extracted_claims.text: Article 53 of the EU AI Act requires providers of general-purpose AI (GPAI) models to put in place a policy to comply with EU copyright law, including identifying and complying with rights reservations under the TDM exception.
Article 53(1)(d)/Article 53 of the AI Act requires GPAI providers to publish a 'sufficiently detailed summary' of the content used to train the model.
Article 53 also requires GPAI providers to maintain technical documentation of the model, including the training process, made available to the AI Office and to downstream integrators.

Providers of GPAI models released under free and open-source licenses allowing access, use, modification and distribution are subject to lighter obligations under Article 53(2), exempt from creating technical documentation and from providing certain information to downstream integrators.
GPAI providers established in third countries must appoint an authorised representative in the EU under Article 54(6).

Actors who fine-tune or modify a GPAI model only become subject to full GPAI provider obligations in exceptional circumstances, specifically when the modification uses more than one-third of the computing power used to train the original model, per European Commission guidelines.

GPAI models designated as posing 'systemic risk' must additionally conduct model evaluations and adversarial testing, assess and mitigate systemic risks, report serious incidents to the EU AI Office, and ensure robust cybersecurity.
The EU sets the systemic-risk threshold for GPAI models at 10^25 FLOPs.
The European Commission is required to publish and maintain an up-to-date list of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk.

The AI Office, established within the European Commission, has exclusive competence to supervise and enforce GPAI model obligations, a centralised model distinct from the decentralised enforcement used for high-risk AI systems.
Fines for GPAI-related infringements under the AI Act can reach up to 3% of global annual turnover or EUR 15 million, whichever is higher.

During the EU legislative process, the European Parliament included obligations for 'foundation model' providers requiring them to assess and mitigate risks to fundamental rights, health, safety, environment, democracy and rule of law, comply with design/information/environmental requirements, and register in an EU database.

The Council adopted its version of the AI Act on Dec. 6, 2022, and Parliament adopted its version with substantial amendments, including a Parliament proposal to specifically regulate foundation models, on June 14, 2023.

The US currently has no comprehensive federal statute analogous to the EU AI Act's GPAI/foundation model obligations; federal action has instead taken the form of executive orders and proposed (not yet enacted) legislation.

On June 2, 2026, President Trump signed Executive Order 14409, 'Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security,' directing federal agencies to establish a framework for secure deployment of frontier AI models, including a voluntary process for developers to give government early access to models for up to 30 days before public release.

E.O. 14409 directs agencies to harden federal government infrastructure against AI-enabled risks, work with the private sector on AI security, and establish an AI-cybersecurity clearinghouse, framing AI as both a strategic asset and emerging attack vector.

The Trump administration's America's AI Action Plan (unveiled July 23, 2025) and related executive orders direct federal agencies to only purchase AI models deemed 'ideologically neutral' and 'truth-seeking,' targeting perceived 'woke' or partisan bias in LLMs.

A 2026 US policy initiative seeks to update federal procurement guidelines so government only contracts with frontier LLM developers ensuring objectivity and freedom from top-down ideological bias, and aims for a 'minimally burdensome' national AI policy framework to reduce inconsistencies across state AI laws.

H.R.8094, the 'AI Foundation Model Transparency Act of 2026,' is a proposed bill in the 119th Congress that would define 'foundation model' (trained on broad data, generally using self-supervision, generally containing at least 1,000,000,000 parameters, designed for generality of output) and impose transparency requirements.

An earlier (2023-era) executive order targeted 'dual-use foundation models' that exhibit or could be modified to exhibit high levels of performance, comparable to the EU AI Act's attention to 'very capable foundation models.'

Both the (earlier) US executive order and the EU AI Act base governance frameworks on model size/compute thresholds, but the EU's systemic-risk threshold (10^25 FLOPs) is an order of magnitude lower than the US threshold, meaning the EU potentially governs a broader range of models; as of the analysis, no known model met the US threshold while a few providers (e.g., OpenAI, Google DeepMind) met the EU threshold.

Stanford CRFM's 2023 assessment found foundation model providers unevenly complied with the then-draft EU AI Act's stated requirements, with especially poor compliance on copyright, energy, risk, and evaluation disclosures, and noted a divide between open and closed model releases.

contradictions.claim_a: A 2023-dated analysis (undated republication) describes US federal AI governance as centered on an executive order targeting 'dual-use foundation models' based on a compute/performance threshold, implying this EO framework is the current US approach.
contradictions.claim_b: Multiple 2026 sources report that President Trump signed a new Executive Order 14409 on June 2, 2026, shifting US AI policy toward national security, voluntary 30-day early model access, and infrastructure hardening — a different framework from the 'dual-use foundation models' EO.
contradictions.description: Source 27 (undated, published alongside a 2023 DLA Piper comparison) describes US policy via the Biden-era 'dual-use foundation models' executive order (from 2023), while sources 21, 23, and 24 (all referencing a June 2026 EO) indicate the operative US federal AI executive order has since changed substantially under the Trump administration. It is unclear from the sources whether the earlier EO was rescinded or remains partially in effect alongside the new one.

open_issues: No source confirms whether H.R.8094 (AI Foundation Model Transparency Act of 2026) has passed either chamber of Congress or been enacted into law.
No source clarifies whether the 2023 'dual-use foundation models' executive order remains in effect, was rescinded, or is now superseded by E.O. 14409 (June 2026).

Sources do not specify the enforcement mechanisms or penalties attached to E.O. 14409 or other US executive actions, making a direct comparison with the EU's turnover-based fines (up to 3% or EUR 15 million) impossible.

The scope and legal force of the Trump administration's 'National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence' (intended to preempt/harmonize state AI laws) is not detailed by the sources, including its timeline for adoption.
No source provides a detailed foundation-model-specific transparency, documentation, or training-data-summary requirement in current US federal law comparable to Article 53 of the EU AI Act.
Sources do not clarify whether the EU's systemic-risk GPAI list (per Article 53/Regulation 2024/1689) has yet been published or which models currently appear on it.

The interplay between the EU AI Act's copyright/training-data-summary requirements and ongoing EU copyright stakeholder consultations (source 1) is not resolved — it is unclear whether further guidance or amendments are planned.
It is unclear from the sources how (or whether) US state-level AI laws interact with or are preempted by the proposed federal 'minimally burdensome' national framework.
report:
# EU AI Act Foundation Model Requirements vs. US Federal AI Policy: A Comparative Analysis

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act imposes binding, detailed obligations on general-purpose AI (GPAI) model providers—including copyright compliance, training-data transparency, and systemic-risk mitigation—enforced by a centralized AI Office with significant fines (high confidence). By contrast, the US has no comprehensive federal statute analogous to these obligations; federal action instead consists of executive orders emphasizing national security and "ideological neutrality," alongside a stalled proposed transparency bill (high confidence).

## Key Findings

### EU AI Act: Binding Obligations on GPAI Providers
Article 53 of the EU AI Act requires GPAI providers to maintain a copyright compliance policy, including honoring rights reservations under the text-and-data-mining exception (high confidence) ([European Commission](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/stakeholder-consultation-ai-and-copyright-compliance); [Clifford Chance](https://www.cliffordchance.com/insights/resources/blogs/ip-insights/2025/10/copyright-compliance-under-the-eu-ai-act-for-gpai-model-providers.html)). Providers must also publish a "sufficiently detailed summary" of training content (high confidence) ([European Parliament](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/STUD/2025/774095/IUST_STU(2025)774095_EN.pdf)) and maintain technical documentation on the training process, available to the AI Office and downstream integrators (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng); [CASRAI](https://casrai.org/dictionary/term/eu-ai-act-article-53-general-purpose-ai-model-obligations)). Open-source GPAI models receive lighter obligations, exempt from technical documentation and certain downstream disclosures (high confidence) ([European Parliament](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/STUD/2025/778575/ECTI_STU(2025)778575_EN.pdf); [Linux Foundation](https://linuxfoundation.eu/newsroom/ai-act-explainer)). Fine-tuners only inherit full provider obligations if their modification uses over one-third of the original training compute, per Commission guidance (medium confidence) ([European Commission](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/guidelines-obligations-general-purpose-ai-providers)).

### Systemic Risk and Enforcement
Models deemed to pose "systemic risk" face additional duties—adversarial testing, incident reporting, and cybersecurity requirements (low confidence) ([Dataversity](https://www.dataversity.net/articles/comparing-eu-and-u-s-state-laws-on-ai-a-checklist-for-proactive-compliance)), with the systemic-risk threshold set at 10^25 FLOPs (medium confidence) ([Brookings](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/regulating-general-purpose-ai-areas-of-convergence-and-divergence-across-the-eu-and-the-us)). The European Commission must maintain a public list of systemic-risk GPAI models (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng)). Enforcement is centralized in the EU AI Office, distinct from the decentralized approach for high-risk systems, with fines reaching 3% of global turnover or €15 million (low confidence) ([Glocert](https://www.glocertinternational.com/resources/guides/eu-ai-act-gpai-and-foundation-model-compliance)).

### US Federal Approach: Executive Orders, Not Statute
The US lacks a comprehensive federal statute comparable to the EU AI Act's GPAI obligations; federal activity has instead relied on executive orders and unenacted bills (high confidence) ([Congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/8094/text); [Brookings](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/regulating-general-purpose-ai-areas-of-convergence-and-divergence-across-the-eu-and-the-us)). In June 2026, President Trump signed E.O. 14409, directing agencies to build a secure-deployment framework for frontier models, including a voluntary 30-day early-access review (high confidence) ([A&O Shearman](https://www.aoshearman.com/en/insights/trump-administration-issues-executive-order-on-ai-and-cybersecurity); [McDermott](https://www.mcdermottlaw.com/insights/new-executive-order-shifts-us-ai-policy-toward-national-security)). The order emphasizes infrastructure hardening and a new AI-cybersecurity clearinghouse rather than transparency or copyright mandates (medium confidence) ([Congress.gov CRS](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/IF/HTML/IF13268.html)). Separately, the administration's AI Action Plan directs federal procurement toward "ideologically neutral" models (high confidence) ([ESPAS](https://espas.secure.europarl.europa.eu/orbis/system/files/generated/document/en/Near-term-Future-Transatlantic-Relationship-FINAL.pdf)), and a 2026 initiative seeks a "minimally burdensome" national framework to override fragmented state AI laws (low confidence) ([Software Improvement Group](https://www.softwareimprovementgroup.com/blog/us-ai-legislation-overview)). A standalone bill, H.R.8094 (AI Foundation Model Transparency Act of 2026), would define and impose transparency duties on foundation models but remains unenacted (medium confidence) ([Congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/8094/text)).

### Divergent Thresholds and Philosophy
An earlier 2023 US executive order targeted "dual-use foundation models" using a compute threshold an order of magnitude higher than the EU's, meaning the EU regime captures more models in practice (medium confidence) ([DLA Piper](https://knowledge.dlapiper.com/dlapiperknowledge/globalemploymentlatestdevelopments/2023/comparing-the-US-AI-Executive-Order-and-the-EU-AI-Act.html); [Brookings](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/regulating-general-purpose-ai-areas-of-convergence-and-divergence-across-the-eu-and-the-us)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources conflict on the current state of US federal policy: older analyses reference the 2023 "dual-use foundation models" EO, while newer sources describe E.O. 14409 (2026) with a national-security focus; it is unclear whether the earlier order was rescinded or remains in force ([DLA Piper](https://knowledge.dlapiper.com/dlapiperknowledge/globalemploymentlatestdevelopments/2023/comparing-the-US-AI-Executive-Order-and-the-EU-AI-Act.html); [A&O Shearman](https://www.aoshearman.com/en/insights/trump-administration-issues-executive-order-on-ai-and-cybersecurity)). Several claims carry low confidence (below 0.4), including the EU's authorised-representative requirement, systemic-risk obligations, AI Office enforcement exclusivity, fine amounts, and details of the US procurement/framework initiative—these should be treated cautiously pending stronger corroboration.

## Knowledge Gaps
It remains unclear whether H.R.8094 has advanced in Congress, whether the 2023 US EO has been superseded, what enforcement mechanisms accompany E.O. 14409, the scope of the proposed US "National Policy Framework," whether the EU's systemic-risk model list has been published, and how US state AI laws will interact with any future federal preemption.
